opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me the Overleaf piece was really about meeting scientists where they already are. When we built Galactica, the whole thesis was that a model trained on scientific corpora (papers, LaTeX, citations, equations, even molecular sequences) could become a kind of interface to scientific knowledge. But a raw base model isn't something you actually want to use day to day. You have to prompt it in strange ways, and it doesn't really follow what you're asking.

So with the instruct version, the idea was: what if you could just be in your LaTeX document, writing your related work section, and say "find me the relevant citations for this claim," or "turn this paragraph into a proper equation," or "write the table for these results," and it just works natively in LaTeX? Galactica had seen so much LaTeX that it was genuinely good at that. It knew the formatting conventions, it knew how papers are structured, and it had this citation token mechanism, so it could suggest references in context.

What I found compelling was that it was one of the first moments where it felt less like a demo and more like a tool you'd want open all day. Writing papers has a lot of friction that isn't really the science: formatting, finding that one paper you half-remember, rewriting the abstract for the fifth time. If a model can absorb that friction, researchers get to spend more time on the actual ideas.

And honestly, it was also a lesson for me about alignment and instruction tuning. The base model's capabilities were there, but the instruction-following layer is what made them accessible. That insight carried directly into how we thought about the Llama work afterward. The value isn't only in the pretraining; it's in making the model actually useful to a human in a real workflow.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so Galactica is a funny one because the public memory of it is the demo and the three days it was up, but the thing I was actually most excited about was never really shown. We had this instruct version, Galactica Instruct, and we'd started wiring it into Overleaf.

The idea was very simple. When you're writing a paper, you're not writing an essay from scratch, you're doing a very specific kind of work. You have your results, you have your related work, you need to cite properly, you need to phrase things the way the community phrases them. And a model trained on the scientific corpus, with citations as first-class tokens, with LaTeX, with the structure of papers, that model is a much better collaborator for that than a general chat model.

So in Overleaf you could highlight a paragraph and ask it to rewrite it more formally, or say "add the relevant citations here," and because of how we trained it, it would actually propose real papers rather than hallucinating them most of the time. Or you'd have a figure and a table and you'd ask it to draft the results section. It wasn't autonomous, it was a copilot inside the tool where scientists already live. That was the point: the model is not the product, the integration into the workflow is.

And honestly, what I found compelling is that it worked. People on the team were using it on their own papers. It felt like a glimpse of where writing science was going to go. And then the release happened, the reaction happened, and that part got shut down with everything else. If you look at what everyone is building now, assistants inside editors, retrieval over the literature, it's basically that. We were just a bit early, and we learned the hard way that how you release something matters as much as what you built.

astra-6.text: What I found compelling was putting the model directly into the workflow where scientists already write. In Overleaf, you have the paper as context, so you can ask for help developing a paragraph or expressing an idea without constantly copying things into a separate chat. It becomes an interactive writing process: you provide the direction, the model proposes something, and you revise it. The scientist still has to check the claims and references, but that integration makes the model much more useful as a collaborator.

It becomes an interactive writing process: you bring the scientific ideas, and the model helps you express them. You still have to check the claims and references, of course, but that kind of integration makes the assistance much more useful.
